title: How I Grew From Engineer to CTO
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Gregor Ojstersek traces his path from self-taught programmer to CTO and uses each step to draw out a lesson about growing into leadership. He credits freelance work, mentoring and consulting with accelerating his growth, and argues that attitude (ownership, drive to improve, making others better) matters more than a degree. The most useful stretch is the middle: feeling stuck as a senior engineer because the next step was undefined, being offered team lead and learning that what made him a good individual contributor did not carry over, and over-thinking people decisions that should have been made quickly and reversed if wrong. Scaling from one team to five or more taught him that process and cross-team collaboration have to be ready before the organisation grows. The close drifts into newsletter growth figures and promotion, but the career narrative itself is a candid account of the engineer-to-manager transition.
points: Being a strong individual contributor did not prepare him for team lead, and he names the first months of management as a struggle.
He stagnated as a senior engineer because he had no defined next step, and he warns that overthinking the path stalls growth.
He over-thought and delayed early people decisions, concluding that it is better to decide faster and reverse course if needed.
Leading five or more teams showed that scaling an organisation without ready processes and clear ownership backfires and slows teams down.
Freelance projects, coaching and consulting alongside the full-time job gave him a broader range of situations to learn from.
quotes: Before that interview, I designed + coded a new website for them. I designed it with Photoshop and built it with HTML + CSS + JS and a bit of PHP. They liked it and gave me good feedback and they offered me the position.
This has sped up my growth substantially. I would not learn as much as I have if I were only focusing on full-time roles.

I thought that people, who have CS Degrees were so good at programming, that I’ll never be on that level. But then, the more people I worked with, the more I knew that my motivation and drive prevails any university knowledge.
These types of decisions were not so easy for me at that time, it took a lot of mental energy and I quite over-thought these decisions. I’ve procrastinated a bit with them.
The company especially needed someone to streamline the process and ensure that the tech team was aligned with the business. That’s exactly one of my main strengths and it was a great fit for me.

Even though my progression may seem linear, it was hardly like that. There were many ups and downs and I’ve made a lot of mistakes, especially when I was a Senior Software Engineer, I was kind of "stuck" and didn't know which path to pursue further.
